q: Which 1960s sitcom starred a talking horse?
fact: Mister Ed's real name was Bamboo Harvester, and he had a great love of peppermints.

q: Who played the sheriff of Mayberry?
fact: That famous whistled theme song was whistled by composer Earle Hagen himself.

q: On Bewitched, Samantha twitched what to cast a spell?
fact: Elizabeth Montgomery's little nose twitch became one of TV's most copied moves.

q: On I Dream of Jeannie, what was Tony Nelson's job?
fact: Jeannie's bottle was really a Jim Beam holiday decanter, painted up for TV.

q: Which family struck oil and moved to Beverly Hills?
fact: The Beverly Hillbillies was the most-watched show in America two years running.

q: Gilligan's Island began with a boat trip meant to last how long?
fact: The little boat that started it all was named the S.S. Minnow.

q: Which show sent a city couple to live on a farm?
fact: Eddie Albert loved gardening and farming in real life, long before Green Acres.

q: Where did the Cartwright family live on Bonanza?
fact: Bonanza was filmed in color partly to help sell America its first color TV sets.

q: Who hosted the Sunday night 'really big show'?
fact: Ed Sullivan introduced the Beatles to about 73 million Americans in one night.

q: Who was Batman's crime-fighting sidekick?
fact: The 1966 Batman flashed words like Pow! and Bam! right across the screen.

q: Who was captain of the Starship Enterprise?
fact: Star Trek ran only three seasons, then became a bigger hit in reruns.

q: What kind of dog was Lassie?
fact: Every Lassie on television was actually played by a male dog.

q: Which cartoon family lived in Bedrock?
fact: Alan Reed invented 'Yabba dabba doo' from his mother's saying, 'A little dab'll do ya.'

q: Which cartoon family lived in the space age?
fact: Rosie the robot maid did all the housework the Jetsons never had to touch.

q: Which cartoon Great Dane solved mysteries with his friends?
fact: Scooby's gang rode around in a flowery van called the Mystery Machine.

q: Rocky the flying squirrel's best pal was what animal?
fact: Bullwinkle was named after a California car dealer named Bulwinkel.

q: Who hosted The Twilight Zone?
fact: Rod Serling wrote more than 90 of the show's episodes himself.

q: On Get Smart, where did Maxwell Smart hide his phone?
fact: Don Adams' shoe phone was a joke decades before anybody carried a real one.

q: Which TV band sang 'Daydream Believer'?
fact: Hundreds of hopefuls answered the open casting call to become a Monkee.

q: On The Addams Family, Thing was a what?
fact: Thing popped out of boxes all over the house, always ready to lend a hand.

q: Which show starred Dick Van Dyke as a TV comedy writer?
fact: Mary Tyler Moore was only 24 years old when she was cast as Laura Petrie.

q: Which spy show's tape self-destructed in five seconds?
fact: Lalo Schifrin wrote that drumbeat theme in an unusual five-beat rhythm.

q: Whose show featured 'champagne music' and floating bubbles?
fact: Lawrence Welk's bubble machine got nearly as famous as his accordion.

q: How did Carol Burnett say goodnight at the end of her show?
fact: The ear tug was a secret hello to her grandmother, watching at home.

q: 'Sock it to me' was a catchphrase on which show?
fact: Goldie Hawn got her start giggling her way through the jokes on Laugh-In.

q: Who hosted Let's Make a Deal?
fact: Fans dressed as bananas and chickens hoping Monty would call on them.

q: On Jeopardy!, players give their answer in the form of a what?
fact: Jeopardy! first aired in 1964 with a friendly host named Art Fleming.

q: Who sat in the center square on Hollywood Squares?
fact: Paul Lynde's giggle from that center square made the whole show sparkle.

q: Which quarterback promised a Jets win in the 1969 Super Bowl?
fact: Joe Namath made his bold promise poolside, then went out and delivered.

q: Julie Andrews sang on a mountaintop in which movie?
fact: The helicopter filming that opening shot kept blowing Julie Andrews over.

q: In Mary Poppins, what did Mary use to fly?
fact: Walt Disney chased the rights to Mary Poppins for about twenty years.

q: Audrey Hepburn ate breakfast in front of which famous store?
fact: That little black dress became the most famous dress in movie history.

q: Who played James Bond in Dr. No?
fact: Sean Connery worked as a milkman and a lifeguard before he became 007.

q: Which Disney movie had 99 spotted puppies?
fact: Animators drew more than six million spots to finish that movie.

q: Baloo sang 'The Bare Necessities' in which Disney film?
fact: Phil Harris improvised so many of Baloo's jokes that they kept them in.

q: Who bumbled through the Pink Panther films as Inspector Clouseau?
fact: The cartoon panther from the opening credits earned his own TV show.

q: Which musical had Jets and Sharks dancing in New York?
fact: West Side Story won ten Academy Awards, a record for a movie musical.

q: Who played Professor Higgins in My Fair Lady?
fact: Rex Harrison insisted on singing live on set instead of lip-syncing.

q: Paul Newman and Robert Redford rode together in which 1969 film?
fact: 'Raindrops Keep Fallin' on My Head' came from that sunny bicycle scene.

q: Elizabeth Taylor played which Egyptian queen in 1963?
fact: Elizabeth Taylor wore 65 different costumes in that one movie.

q: Which Elvis movie was set in Hawaii?
fact: 'Can't Help Falling in Love' came straight out of Blue Hawaii.

q: 'Lara's Theme' came from which sweeping 1965 film?
fact: The melody got so popular it became the song 'Somewhere, My Love.'

q: Barbra Streisand won an Oscar playing Fanny Brice in what?
fact: It was her first movie, and she tied for Best Actress with Katharine Hepburn.

q: Which team won the very first Super Bowl in 1967?
fact: Vince Lombardi's Packers made little Green Bay famous as Titletown.

q: Who was known as the master of suspense?
fact: Hitchcock slipped a quick cameo of himself into nearly every film he made.

q: Which Mouseketeer grew up to star in beach party movies?
fact: Walt Disney spotted Annette dancing at a recital in Burbank and hired her.

q: Which city was the home of Motown Records?
fact: Berry Gordy started Motown with an $800 loan from his family.

q: Diana Ross was the lead singer of which group?
fact: The Supremes racked up a dozen number one hits in their heyday.

q: 'My Girl' was a hit for which Motown group?
fact: Smokey Robinson wrote 'My Girl' especially for the Temptations.

q: Which English city were the Beatles from?
fact: Thousands of screaming fans met their plane when they landed in New York.

q: Which band sang about surfing and California girls?
fact: Only one Beach Boy, Dennis Wilson, actually knew how to surf.

q: Chubby Checker got the whole country doing which dance?
fact: 'The Twist' went to number one twice, in 1960 and again in 1962.

q: Who was called the Queen of Soul?
fact: Aretha made 'Respect' entirely her own, and it became an anthem.

q: Nancy Sinatra sang about boots made for doing what?
fact: Frank Sinatra's daughter got her very first number one hit with that song.

q: Which singer was known as the Man in Black?
fact: June Carter helped write 'Ring of Fire,' one of his biggest hits.

q: Mickey Mantle spent his whole career with which team?
fact: Mickey Mantle could hit home runs batting either righty or lefty.

q: Simon and Garfunkel sang 'The Sound of' what?
fact: The two met in grade school in Queens and were singing together as teens.

q: Petula Clark invited everyone to go where in her 1964 hit?
fact: Songwriter Tony Hatch got the idea walking through the lights of New York.

q: Which crooner sang 'Moon River' on his own TV show?
fact: 'Moon River' was written for a movie and went on to win an Oscar.

q: Which Motown star recorded 'Fingertips' as a young teenager?
fact: He played harmonica on it, and the live crowd absolutely roared.

q: 'Dancing in the Street' was a hit for Martha and the what?
fact: Martha Reeves was a Motown secretary before she got her chance to sing.

q: Frank Sinatra had a 1966 hit about strangers in the what?
fact: Sinatra never much liked the song, but it won him a Grammy anyway.

q: Ray Charles sang about which state being on his mind?
fact: Georgia later made his version the official state song.

q: The Righteous Brothers sang 'You've Lost That Lovin'' what?
fact: It is said to be the most played song in American radio history.

q: Tammy Wynette's biggest hit told women to stand by their what?
fact: Tammy and her producer wrote the whole thing in about twenty minutes.

q: Which country star sang 'Wichita Lineman'?
fact: Jimmy Webb wrote it after passing a lone lineman on a pole in Oklahoma.

q: The Mamas and the Papas were dreaming of which state?
fact: 'California Dreamin'' was written on a freezing winter day in New York.

q: What did shoppers paste into books to trade for prizes?
fact: S&H once printed more stamps every year than the U.S. Post Office did.

q: Which sporty Ford arrived in 1964 and sold like crazy?
fact: Ford sold a million Mustangs in well under two years.

q: What was the friendly nickname for the Volkswagen Beetle?
fact: The Bug's engine sat in the back, so the trunk was up front.

q: Where did families park the car to watch a movie?
fact: At their peak, America had more than four thousand drive-in theaters.

q: Which frozen supper came on a divided metal tray?
fact: Swanson sold ten million TV dinners in the very first year.

q: Which orange drink mix went along with the astronauts?
fact: Tang was already on grocery shelves, but the space program made it famous.

q: Which toaster pastry arrived in 1964?
fact: The very first Pop-Tarts had no frosting on them at all.

q: Whose golf fans were known as 'Arnie's Army'?
fact: Arnold Palmer's easy charm helped bring golf onto television screens.

q: 'Plop, plop, fizz, fizz' sold which product?
fact: Sales jumped once the ads showed two tablets dropping instead of one.

q: Which giggling doughboy popped out of a can in 1965?
fact: His name is Poppin' Fresh, and he has been giggling ever since.

q: 'Please don't squeeze the ___,' scolded Mr. Whipple.
fact: Actor Dick Wilson played Mr. Whipple for more than twenty years.

q: Which tuna kept hearing 'Sorry, Charlie'?
fact: Charlie had good taste, but StarKist wanted tuna that tastes good.

q: Which cereal mascot roared 'They're gr-r-reat!'?
fact: Thurl Ravenscroft gave Tony that mighty voice for over fifty years.

q: Which doll got a boyfriend named Ken in 1961?
fact: Barbie and Ken were named after the toymaker's own two children.

q: Which 1964 toy was 'America's movable fighting man'?
fact: His makers coined the phrase 'action figure' so boys could play with dolls.

q: Which party game put players on a big polka-dot mat?
fact: Twister took off after Johnny Carson played it on The Tonight Show.

q: Which little cars raced on orange track starting in 1968?
fact: Hot Wheels had special red-striped tires and rolled faster than anything.

q: Which boxer famously called himself 'The Greatest'?
fact: He described his own style as float like a butterfly, sting like a bee.

q: Which short skirt was the daring new look of the 1960s?
fact: London designer Mary Quant named it after her favorite car, the Mini.

q: Which tall, teased hairdo was named after a bee's home?
fact: A Chicago hairdresser dreamed up the beehive back in 1960.

q: What did Neil Armstrong do in July of 1969?
fact: About 600 million people around the world watched him take that first step.

q: Who walked on the moon alongside Neil Armstrong?
fact: Buzz Aldrin looked around and called the view 'magnificent desolation.'

q: What was the name of the Apollo 11 lunar module?
fact: 'The Eagle has landed' told the whole world they had made it safely.

q: Which TV family toured in a brightly painted bus?
fact: Shirley Jones, who played the mom, was David Cassidy's real-life stepmother.

q: How did the Waltons say goodnight?
fact: That gentle goodnight became so famous that fans said it to each other.

q: How many children were in the Brady Bunch?
fact: Six kids shared one bathroom, and a toilet was never once shown on screen.

q: What was the Bradys' housekeeper's name?
fact: Ann B. Davis had already won two Emmys before she put on Alice's apron.

q: Who played the Fonz on Happy Days?
fact: Henry Winkler couldn't ride a motorcycle, so the Fonz mostly posed on it.

q: Where did the Happy Days gang hang out?
fact: Happy Days grew out of one segment on the show Love, American Style.

q: Laverne and Shirley worked at a what?
fact: Their bouncy opening chant came from a sidewalk rhyme Penny Marshall knew as a girl.

q: Mary Tyler Moore famously tossed what into the air?
fact: That happy hat toss was filmed on a busy street in downtown Minneapolis.

q: Which show starred Redd Foxx as a junk dealer?
fact: Redd Foxx named his character after his own brother, Fred Sanford.

q: The Jeffersons were 'movin' on up' to where?
fact: Ja'net DuBois co-wrote and belted out that theme song herself.

q: Which TV detective wore a rumpled raincoat?
fact: Peter Falk bought that raincoat himself and wore it for decades.

q: Which bald TV detective was always sucking a lollipop?
fact: Telly Savalas asking 'Who loves ya, baby?' became a national catchphrase.

q: Which show had three women working for a mystery boss?
fact: Farrah Fawcett's smiling poster sold around twelve million copies.

q: Steve Austin was rebuilt for how much money?
fact: Slow motion made him look superfast, and every kid in America copied it.

q: Who played Wonder Woman on television?
fact: That spin-into-costume twirl was invented just for the TV show.

q: Which friendly alien said 'Nanu, nanu'?
fact: Robin Williams improvised so much that scripts left blank space for him.

q: On Fantasy Island, who announced the arriving plane?
fact: Hervé Villechaize shouting 'De plane!' opened every single episode.

q: The Love Boat took place aboard what?
fact: Episodes were filmed aboard real Princess cruise ships at sea.

q: Which frog hosted The Muppet Show?
fact: Jim Henson made the very first Kermit out of his mother's old coat.

q: Who was Kermit's glamorous admirer?
fact: Miss Piggy began as a background pig and karate-chopped her way to stardom.

q: Which show featured a class called the Sweathogs?
fact: A young John Travolta played Vinnie Barbarino before he was a movie star.

q: Which cop show had a red car with a big white stripe?
fact: That Ford Torino picked up the nickname 'the Striped Tomato.'

q: Hawaii Five-O ended episodes with 'Book 'em' who?
fact: That surf-rock theme song became a favorite of marching bands everywhere.

q: Little House on the Prairie came from books by whom?
fact: Michael Landon starred in it, directed it, and wrote many episodes too.

q: Which children's show introduced Big Bird?
fact: Big Bird's sunny costume is made from hundreds of dyed turkey feathers.

q: Who began hosting The Price Is Right in 1972?
fact: 'Come on down!' has been sending people racing to the stage ever since.

q: Which game show surveyed one hundred people?
fact: Host Richard Dawson gave a kiss to nearly every woman on the show.

q: Who hosted American Bandstand for decades?
fact: Dick Clark was nicknamed 'America's oldest teenager,' and he earned it.

q: Which dance show was hosted by Don Cornelius?
fact: The Soul Train line let every dancer show off their very best moves.

q: Which 1977 movie opened 'A long time ago...'?
fact: The little beeping robot had an actor curled up inside him.

q: Which movie boxer ran up the steps in Philadelphia?
fact: Sylvester Stallone wrote the script in about three days and insisted on starring.

q: Travolta and Newton-John sang together in which 1978 film?
fact: Olivia Newton-John was 29 years old playing a high school senior.

q: Which group's songs powered Saturday Night Fever?
fact: That soundtrack sold more than forty million copies around the world.

q: Gene Wilder ran a magical factory that made what?
fact: His famous limp-then-somersault entrance was entirely his own idea.

q: Which Mel Brooks comedy spoofed old monster movies?
fact: They filmed it using the actual laboratory props from the 1931 original.

q: Burt Reynolds drove a black Trans Am in which movie?
fact: Pontiac could barely build Trans Ams fast enough after that movie came out.

q: Who played Superman in the 1978 movie?
fact: Christopher Reeve was an unknown stage actor when he won the part.

q: The Sting brought back piano music by which composer?
fact: 'The Entertainer' was seventy years old and suddenly a top ten hit.

q: Which 1973 film looked back on cruising in 1962?
fact: A young Harrison Ford and a young Ron Howard were both in the cast.

q: Streisand and Redford starred in which 1973 romance?
fact: The title song went all the way to number one on the charts.

q: Which musical film featured Tevye and his daughters?
fact: It won three Academy Awards, including one for that beautiful music.

q: Which Disney cartoon told Robin Hood's story with animals?
fact: Robin was a clever fox and Little John was a great big friendly bear.

q: Which theme park opened in Florida in 1971?
fact: Cinderella Castle stands 189 feet tall, much taller than Disneyland's.

q: Kermit sang 'Rainbow Connection' in which 1979 film?
fact: The song earned a nomination for an Academy Award.

q: Which Swedish group sang 'Dancing Queen'?
fact: ABBA's name is just the first letters of the four singers' first names.

q: Which brother-and-sister duo sang 'Close to You'?
fact: Karen Carpenter started out sitting behind the drums, not at the microphone.

q: Who sang 'Take Me Home, Country Roads'?
fact: West Virginia later made it one of its official state songs.

q: Who sang about a red-haired woman named Jolene?
fact: Dolly says she borrowed the name from a little red-haired girl she once met.

q: 'The Gambler' was a big hit for which singer?
fact: Kenny Rogers turned that one song into a whole run of TV movies.

q: Glen Campbell sang about which kind of cowboy in 1975?
fact: It went to number one and became his signature song for good.

q: Which group sang 'Hotel California'?
fact: The Eagles' greatest hits album became one of the best sellers of all time.

q: Who was crowned the Queen of Disco?
fact: Donna Summer sang in musical theater long before she ever set foot in a disco.

q: 'I Will Survive' was a disco anthem for whom?
fact: It was tucked away as the B-side until DJs flipped the record over.

q: Which group spelled out 'Y.M.C.A.' with their arms?
fact: Those arm letters were invented by the fans, not by the band.

q: Which young family group sang 'ABC'?
fact: Their first four singles all went straight to number one.

q: Which flashy singer wore glittery glasses at the piano?
fact: Elton John owned so many pairs of glasses they could fill a whole room.

q: Barry Manilow's 'Copacabana' was about what kind of place?
fact: Barry got his start writing those catchy little jingles for TV commercials.

q: Simon and Garfunkel's 1970 hit was 'Bridge Over Troubled' what?
fact: It took home both Record of the Year and Song of the Year at the Grammys.

q: Who sang 'Ain't No Mountain High Enough' in 1970?
fact: It was her first solo number one after leaving the Supremes.

q: Which pet needed no feeding and came in a little box?
fact: The Pet Rock made its inventor a millionaire in about six months.

q: Which ring supposedly changed color with your mood?
fact: The stone was really just reacting to the warmth of your finger.

q: What did CB radio users say to mean 'got it'?
fact: Everybody picked a CB 'handle,' a nickname just for the airwaves.

q: Which flared trousers defined 1970s style?
fact: The wider the bell, the better, especially over a pair of platform shoes.

q: Which knotted craft made those hanging plant holders?
fact: If a house had a spider plant, it was probably swinging in macramé.

q: Which appliance color absolutely screamed 1970s?
fact: Avocado green and harvest gold ruled American kitchens for a decade.

q: Which tape format clunked loudly in the middle of a song?
fact: That clunk when the 8-track changed programs was part of the charm.

q: Which slow cooker arrived in kitchens in 1971?
fact: Supper cooked itself all day long while everybody was out of the house.

q: 'You deserve a break today' belonged to which restaurant?
fact: It is often called one of the best advertising jingles ever written.

q: 'Have it your way' was the promise of which burger chain?
fact: The jingle cheerfully offered to hold the pickles and hold the lettuce.

q: Which cereal ad asked little Mikey to try it?
fact: The Mikey commercial kept running for more than a decade.

q: 'Leggo my Eggo' was about which breakfast food?
fact: Eggo got its name because the waffles tasted so nice and eggy.

q: Which candy crackled and popped on your tongue?
fact: A chemist trying to invent instant soda pop came up with them by accident.

q: Which haircut did skater Dorothy Hamill make famous?
fact: Girls everywhere carried her picture into the salon in 1976.

q: Which horse won the Triple Crown in 1973?
fact: Secretariat won the Belmont by 31 lengths, and that record still stands.

q: Who broke Babe Ruth's career home run record in 1974?
fact: Hank Aaron's 715th homer sailed over the wall in Atlanta.

q: Which gymnast scored the first perfect 10 in 1976?
fact: The scoreboard couldn't display 10.00, so it flashed 1.00 instead.

q: Which swimmer won seven gold medals in 1972?
fact: Mark Spitz did it all while sporting his famous mustache.

q: What big birthday did America celebrate in 1976?
fact: Tall ships sailed into New York Harbor and fireworks lit up every town.

q: Which wood-sided family car hauled everyone to the lake?
fact: Kids always fought over the rear-facing back seat, the very best spot.

q: Which 1972 game brought table tennis to the TV screen?
fact: Pong was so popular in bars that the machines jammed full of quarters.
